extracted.intended_audience: readers or writers studying satirical/renaissance comedy (e.g., Rabelais), humorists learning comic techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and standards for producing coarse, satirical, Rabelaisian-style humor that mixes high register parody, bodily/scatological comedy, hyperbolic catalogues, and surreal imagery. Useful for authors or analysts of grotesque satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock-praise / ironic encomium of institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use solemn, exalted language to praise an institution or book (here, the 'sacred decretals') while the surrounding details and context reveal the praise as absurd and satirical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Homenas's long, increasingly extravagant praises of the decretals ('O seraphic Sextum!... O angelical Extravagantes!...'), attributing worldly power and miraculous benefits to them. Guidance: adopt an inflated, reverent tone and then undercut it with concrete, ridiculous consequences (e.g., basins collecting coins for taverns, moral corruption). Anti-pattern: plain mockery without the solemn register loses the ironic contrast; avoid obvious one-liners in place of extended faux-serious encomium.

rubrics_metrics.name: High–low register juxtaposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast elevated (religious, legal, Latinized) diction with crude, bodily, or vulgar material to produce comic dissonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mixing Latin/clerical terms ('pallium, amice, rochet', 'Clementinae') with descriptions of basins, drunkenness, farting, sexual leering. Use learned-sounding phrases next to earthy imagery to magnify absurdity. Anti-pattern: flattening tone so both registers read the same; the humor depends on the perceptible clash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque and bodily (scatological) comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploy vivid descriptions of bodily functions, ailments, and sexualized or excremental detail for comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Friar John's constipation, piles, 'orifice of my nockandroe', farting, leering friar, inoculating with lancets between toes. Guidance: use graphic specificity and escalation to shock and amuse; pair with ironic commentary. Anti-pattern: gratuitous vulgarity without wit or satirical target tends toward offensiveness rather than effective comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long lists / enumeratio for comic escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Accumulate long catalogues of items, punishments, goods, or verbs to create rhythm, exaggeration, and overwhelm the reader for comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the riotous multicolumn list of tortures/punishments ('Burn ‘em, tear 'em, nip ‘em with hot pincers... carbonade ‘em on gridirons'), lists of ruined garments or spoiled spices, and inventories of miracles. Guidance: build length and cumulative absurdity; break expectations by varying the kinds of items. Anti-pattern: lists that are too short or lack variation lose the escalatory punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurd hyperbole and escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Push claims to ludicrous extremes (world-saving decretals, universities literally protected by books) to lampoon pretension and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claiming decretals bring peace, create emperors, found universities, and draw hundreds of thousands of ducats annually. Guidance: present a series of increasingly improbable consequences to expose the target's vanity or corruption. Anti-pattern: hyperbole that lacks a clear satirical target becomes mere silliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody of learned/official language and pseudo-scholarly voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitate the form and vocabulary of legal, theological, or scholarly discourse (including Latinisms and citations) and use that form to satirize its content or practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: lampooning decretal chapters and ecclesiastical rhetoric, insertion of phrases like 'Execrabilis, De multa, Si plures', mock-scholarly asides. Guidance: use authentic-seeming jargon and then subvert it with concrete incongruities. Anti-pattern: imitation that is shallow or relies on inaccurate jargon can read as nonsensical rather than satirical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification and animating the inanimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Give inanimate things lives or agency (e.g., words freezing and thawing, Orpheus's head singing) to create wonder and comic surrealism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'frozen words' thawing into sounds and onomatopoeia; Orpheus's head still singing. Guidance: use magical-realism devices to create playful, uncanny images that both amuse and carry metaphorical weight. Anti-pattern: personification without a clear payoff can feel arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invented words, onomatopoeia, and phonetic play
rubrics_metrics.description: Include strings of invented sounds, phonetic sequences, and comic noises to produce musicality, absurdity, and visceral humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sequences like 'hin, hin, hin... bredelinbrededack, frr, frr, frr, bou, bou...' used to mimic battle noises and create playful soundscapes. Guidance: vary rhythm and phonemes to surprise readers and to imitate the sounds being described. Anti-pattern: overuse without textual anchor becomes cacophony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and refrain for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use repeated cries, exclamations, or refrains (e.g., 'Miracle!') to build communal comic effect and to punctuate scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Miracle! cried Homenas' recurs after each 'miracle' story; repeated 'O' invocations ('O seraphic Sextum!') create mock-devotion. Guidance: repetition amplifies absurdity and creates a ritualized comedic beat. Anti-pattern: repetition without variation can become monotonous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic misinterpretation, malapropism, and deliberate confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit misunderstandings, near-misses, and linguistic slips (e.g., mistaken words, false etymologies) for comedic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the slip between 'decretist' and 'decretalist', Friar John's mangled Latin or the characters misunderstanding each other and their surroundings. Guidance: stage small lexical errors that reveal character foolishness or institutional pretension. Anti-pattern: errors that confuse the reader rather than revealing character or satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anecdotal tall-tale structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame humor as a sequence of plausible-sounding but increasingly unlikely anecdotes and 'miracles' told by characters to mock credulity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: multiple town anecdotes (tailors' ruined garments, archers missing because of decretal-leaves) presented as eyewitness reports. Guidance: use the teller's apparent seriousness to heighten the absurdity of the tale. Anti-pattern: tales lacking narrative detail or a consistent teller voice may not land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical comedy and stage-like spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe visible, bodily actions, gestures, and interactions (leering, cap-clapping, maidens' songs) as if staging a farce to generate visual humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Friar John leering 'like a cur that steals a capon', maidens clapping on a cap and kissing it, pantomime-like interactions at table. Guidance: render physical actions vividly and time them to speech beats; pair physical comedy with verbal wit. Anti-pattern: describing action flatly without rhythm or sensory detail blunts the comic image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical credentialing and rhetorical questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a rhetorical series of questions and 'what-if' portraits to parody credentialism and the claimed omnipotence of an expertise group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: repeated rhetorical questions 'Would you choose a worthy emperor... Take me a decretalist' that absurdly attribute all state functions to decretalists. Guidance: use mock-logical syllogisms to expose self-serving claims to authority. Anti-pattern: rhetorical lists that lack escalation or irony read as earnest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming and label-play as caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Coin or deploy labels and group names (e.g., 'Pantagruelists', 'decretalicides') to caricature groups and to create satirical neologisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: inventing compound insults and group labels in Latinized or mock-classical form to lampoon enemies ('decretalifuges, decretalicides, decretalictones'). Guidance: craft novel compound words that sound plausibly learned but carry comic insult. Anti-pattern: neologisms that are opaque or lack audible humor won't read as funny.
